parsed.study_design: National cross-sectional household survey and tubewell census
parsed.population_and_sample: Rural households outside the four major metropolitan areas; 3,780 randomly selected households containing 20,260 people, plus a census of 9,174 tubewells in 90 village clusters (analyses restricted to functional wells).
parsed.exposure: Administrative testing and red-marking of arsenic-contaminated tubewells, public/private/community well provision and ownership, and access to alternative safe wells through water-sharing arrangements.
parsed.outcome: Household drinking-water source and access, continued use of condemned wells, actual and preferred switching to alternative water sources, and availability of nearby safe tubewells.
parsed.rationale: The research-program section (pp. 2091–2092) reports two identifiable empirical studies—a nationally sampled household survey and a village-level tubewell census. Tables 1–4 and the “Tubewell water” and “Tubewell option” sections (pp. 2092–2095) quantify access to private and public wells, testing and red-marking, continued use of contaminated wells, and household switching behavior, directly linking an administrative governance intervention to safe-water access outcomes.
